school: Institutional Economics, Development Economics, Welfare Economics
legacy: Gunnar Myrdal was one of the most influential social scientists of the twentieth century. He refused to separate economics from politics, sociology, history, and ethics, arguing that social problems can only be understood through an interdisciplinary approach. His work shaped debates on poverty, race relations, economic development, welfare policy, and inequality. By emphasizing the interaction of economic and social forces, he helped transform development economics and inspired policymakers across the world. His influence extends far beyond economics into sociology, political science, and public policy.
earlyLife: Myrdal was born in rural Sweden and grew up during a period of rapid social and economic transformation. He studied law and economics, becoming increasingly interested in how social institutions influence economic outcomes. Early in his academic career, he questioned the idea that economics could be entirely value-free and argued that researchers should openly acknowledge the moral assumptions underlying their work. These concerns remained central throughout his intellectual life.
scientificField: Economics, Sociology, Development Studies, Public Policy, Social Theory
majorContributions: Myrdal developed the concept of cumulative causation, which argues that economic and social changes often reinforce themselves through feedback loops. According to this view, advantages tend to create further advantages while disadvantages can generate deeper disadvantages unless corrective action is taken. This idea became highly influential in the study of poverty, regional inequality, and economic development. His landmark work 'An American Dilemma' examined the contradiction between democratic ideals and racial discrimination in the United States, helping shape later discussions of civil rights and social justice. He also made important contributions to the analysis of welfare states, economic planning, population policy, and the challenges facing developing nations.
laterLife: During his later career, Myrdal combined academic research with public service and international policy work. He held important governmental and diplomatic positions while continuing to publish influential studies on development, inequality, and social change. His extensive research on Asia and the developing world broadened the scope of development economics and encouraged greater attention to institutions, education, health, and social reform. His intellectual influence continued to grow throughout his life, earning recognition as one of the leading social theorists of his generation.
whyImportant: Myrdal is important because he demonstrated that economic problems cannot be understood in isolation from social and political conditions. His theories highlighted the importance of institutions, education, public policy, and historical context in shaping economic outcomes. Long before inequality became a central topic in contemporary economics, he was analyzing how social structures reproduce privilege and disadvantage. His interdisciplinary perspective continues to influence research on development, social justice, welfare policy, and economic reform.
